title: Surge mitigation & isolation playbook — design sketch
content:
Context:

This is a working sketch for a product + ops playbook to mitigate short, high-intensity traffic surges against Dedicated GPU pools while preserving tenant isolation and predictable SLO behavior. The goal is to provide well-scoped, operator-friendly controls that balance latency SLOs, cost predictability, and tenant fairness for customers on Dedicated plans.

Why this exists (motivation):
- We see recurring incidents where ephemeral spikes from a small subset of tenants exhaust pooled capacity and cause noisy-neighbor latency regressions for other tenants.
- Existing mechanisms (hard throttles, eviction, preemptible fallback) either cause sudden customer-visible failures or are too conservative and waste headroom.
- Need a flexible, observable set of levers that on-call and platform engineers can tune per-tenant or per-pool.

High-level principles:
1) Prefer graceful degradation over abrupt failures: provide clear, measurable tiers of degraded service with bounded impact.
2) Make mitigation reversible and observable: every action should have a short TTL and a rollback path.
3) Minimize manual toil: expose automations with simulated dry-run and telemetry before hard cutovers.
4) Protect high-SLO tenants: tiering should honor customer commitments.

Goals (product + operational):
- Reduce cross-tenant P90 latency spikes during surges by 40% on average across impacted pools.
- Limit customer-visible request errors (HTTP 503/429) during surges to under 1% for paying Dedicated tenants with gold SLAs.
- Provide a small set of orthogonal controls (soft-credits, latency-lanes, burst tokens) that SREs or account teams can tune per-tenant.

Non-goals:
- This doc is not about pricing changes, long-term oversubscription modeling, or per-model kernel-level optimizations. Those are separate efforts.

User stories (examples):
- As an SRE, I want to temporarily shorten the KV-cache TTL for opportunistic tenants to free memory and reduce evictions for gold-tier tenants during a surge.
- As an account manager, I want to borrow short-lived burst credits for a seasonal customer while ensuring baseline isolation for other tenants.
- As a platform operator, I want to automatically shift best-effort traffic to lower-cost preemptible instances when overall pool utilization > 90% without impacting guaranteed lanes.

Proposed controls (sketch):
1) Burst Credit Wallets (per-tenant): short-lived credits consumed during bursts. Credits can be purchased (reserved) or earned (behavioral, e.g., consistent usage pattern).
   - Mechanics: credits translate into ephemeral headroom allocation requests to the pool scheduler.
   - Failure mode: when credits exhausted, traffic falls back to best-effort lanes or is throttled according to policy.

2) Latency Lanes (multi-tier routing): explicitly tag requests into lanes: guaranteed (SLA), standard, opportunistic. Router enforces lane-level admission controls at queueing layer.
   - Router policy: guaranteed always admitted (within reserved capacity), standard admitted if pool utilization < threshold, opportunistic admitted opportunistically.

3) Soft-decommit + Warm-wait: rather than immediate preemption, mark excess pods as soft-decommitable and give them a short grace window (30–90s) to finish in-flight requests or checkpoint KV cache.

4) Adaptive backpressure signals: integrate per-tenant pacing tokens and client-side retry guidance to reduce spike amplification from poorly-behaved clients.

5) Ephemeral overflow routing: traffic over a per-tenant burst threshold can be routed to a configurable overflow cluster (lower-cost preemptible nodes or second-region fallback) with optional response-quality degradation labels.

Operational flows / Runbook (for on-call):
- Detection:
  - Alert: Pool utilization > 85% and P95 latency > 2x baseline for > 2 minutes.
  - Dashboard: show per-tenant QPS, lane breakdown, burst credit consumption, KV cache hit rate.

- Immediate mitigation steps (automated preferred):
  1) Auto-invoke lane admission smoothing: throttle opportunistic lane by 50% for 60s.
  2) If high-priority guaranteed tenants are degraded, invoke soft-decommit for opportunistic pods and trigger ephemeral overflow routing for opportunistic traffic.
  3) Send Slack notice to impacted account owners with actions taken and expected window.

- Escalation:
  - If P95 remains > target after 5 minutes, identify top-3 consumers (by credit consumption or QPS). Consider manual credit quarantine or targeted throttling.
  - If impact persists > 15 minutes, schedule emergency capacity increase (warm additional nodes) or engage on-call infra to add temporary burst-capacity.

Telemetry and SLOs to track:
- Pool level: utilization, headroom left, preemption count, average KV cache eviction rate.
- Tenant level: lane breakdown, burst credit balance, throttled requests, P50/P95/P99 latency per lane.
- Business: % of requests with degraded label, number of SLA violations, number of manual interventions.

UI and API surfaces (product notes):
- Tenant console: show burst credit balance, recent consumption heatmap, ability to purchase/allowlist temporary credits, set preferred overflow cluster.
- Admin console: per-pool control to change lane thresholds, emergency soft-quarantine toggle, manual credit drains.
- Public API: programmatic toggle for overflow behavior and lane hints (for large customers wanting to pass hints via headers).

Safety and customer experience considerations:
- Any mitigation that can return degraded responses (e.g., lower-quality model, shortened context window) must carry an explicit response header and user-visible guidance to avoid silent regression.
- Billing: actions that route traffic to different infra tiers must be tagged for audit; any automatic fallback should not surprise customers on billing — we must indicate cost-impact in the tenant console and post-mortem.

Open design questions / tradeoffs (needs engineering input):
- How fast can the scheduler carve ephemeral headroom without causing fragmentation? (impact on bin-packing)
- What is a safe TTL for soft-decommit to avoid state loss in KV caches for transformer decoders?
- Where to store burst credit ledger so it is extremely low-latency but auditable for billing? (Redis vs transactional DB)
- How to safely test overflow routing in production without exposing customers to degraded models unexpectedly? We probably need canary flags + simulated traffic.

Prototype proposal (MVP):
- Implement lane-level admission controls and an operator endpoint to nudge lane thresholds.
- Add a per-tenant burst credit counter persisted in existing account metadata (read/write with conservative rate limits) and a simple scheduler hook that checks credits when deciding admission for opportunistic requests.
- Build a dashboard panel and a 1-click operator mitigation flow (throttle opportunistic lane / trigger overflow).

Rollout plan (phases):
1) Internal canary: enable in a single dev pool with a small set of internal tenants. Test detection -> automated throttle -> rollback paths.
2) Beta customers: opt-in for 5–10 dedicated customers who want burst behavior; get feedback and iterate.
3) Gradual opt-in: default lane thresholds applied but credits disabled; customers must opt-in to buy/enable credits.

Metrics for success (90 days post-rollout):
- Median cross-tenant P95 latency during surges reduced by 30–50% in enabled pools.
- Operator manual interventions per week reduced by 60% for surge incidents.
- Fewer than 2 significant customer complaints attributed to hidden degradations during first 3 months.

Implementation risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Scheduler complexity increases and harms normal steady-state throughput.
  - Mitigation: Start with conservative thresholds and short-lived experiments; add simulated load testing.
- Risk: Billing surprises from overflow routing.
  - Mitigation: Track and surface any cost-differentials in the console and include explicit customer opt-in for paid overflow consumption.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Product: finalize API surface for credits and lane hints (owner: Monica).
- Eng (Serving runtime): estimate KV-cache checkpointing feasibility for soft-decommit (owner: Ravi).
- SRE: add dashboard panels and an alert rule for combined util+latency (owner: Ethan).
- Legal / Billing: quick review of how to label overflow charges (owner: Priya).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally high-level and ops-focused. Looking for feedback on guardrail values (e.g., credit TTL, soft-decommit window), and whether we should treat overflow routing as an automated action or operator-triggered only for the MVP.
- Please add Jira links to any tech spikes you think should be created; I started ENGINF-2314 for a scheduler spike.

----
Choppy appendix (brainstorm fragments):
- "burst tokens" vs "burst credits" naming: tokens = instantaneous admission, credits = cumulative budget. Prefer credits.
- Could reuse existing reserve/reservation primitives for guaranteed lanes rather than re-inventing.
- Consider integrating client-side SDK guidance — clients could opt into exponential backoff tuned to lane type.
- Quick UX idea: a timeline scrubber in tenant console that shows burst events + credit delta, with links to trace ids.

End of sketch.
